subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In persuasive writing, what is the effect of using a rule of three (a triplet)?
options: It creates rhythm and emphasis, making the point more memorable
It makes the writing harder to read
It signals the end of the piece
It removes the need for evidence
questions.explain: A triplet adds rhythm and emphasis, making ideas stick in the reader's mind.

questions.q: Which technique is being used: 'Imagine a world where no child goes to bed hungry'?
options: A statistic
An anecdote
Direct address and an emotive appeal
A rhetorical question
questions.explain: It speaks directly to the reader ('Imagine') and triggers an emotional response.

questions.q: You are writing a leaflet for a local charity event. Which feature is most appropriate to the form?
options: A single dense block of text
Clear headings, bullet points and key details like time and place
No headings at all
Footnotes and academic citations
questions.explain: Leaflets use headings, bullets and signposting so readers can scan key information quickly.

questions.q: For an article aimed at teenagers about social media, which register is most suitable?
options: Highly formal legal language
Babyish, oversimplified language
A lively, accessible tone with some direct address
Technical scientific jargon throughout
questions.explain: Matching register to a teenage audience means engaging but clear, not stuffy or patronising.

questions.q: Which is the most effective, vivid sensory description of a market?
options: The market was busy and had lots of things.
Spices stung the air, voices clashed overhead, and ripe mangoes glistened on every stall.
There were many people at the market buying food.
The market was a place where you could buy stuff.
questions.explain: It engages multiple senses (smell, sound, sight) to create an immersive image.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The old house was scary and big.
The house was very very scary.
The big house was really old and bad.
The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
To replace punctuation
To add decoration to sentences
To make writing longer
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: She was very nervous about the exam.
The girl was nervous because of the test.
She felt nervous and scared inside.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: You are writing a review of a film. Which feature suits the form best?
options: Stage directions in brackets
A bibliography of academic sources
A balanced judgement supported by specific examples and a recommendation
A formal salutation and address block
questions.explain: Reviews give an evaluative judgement backed by examples and end with a recommendation.

questions.q: You are writing a formal letter to your local council. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: So basically the bins are a nightmare.
I am writing to express my concern about waste collection in our area.
Bins are well annoying, sort it out.
Hey, listen up about these bins!
questions.explain: A formal letter requires a clear, polite statement of purpose in Standard English.

questions.q: Which is the best way to adapt your writing for a young child as the audience?
options: Write in a formal, legalistic register
Include dense statistics and technical jargon
Use long, complex sentences and abstract vocabulary
Use simple, clear sentences, friendly tone and concrete vocabulary
questions.explain: Writing for young children needs simple sentences, a warm tone and accessible words.

questions.q: Which paragraphing choice best helps a reader follow a piece of writing?
options: Never using paragraphs in formal writing
Starting a new paragraph for each new idea, time or place
Beginning a new paragraph after every sentence
Writing the whole piece as one long paragraph
questions.explain: Paragraphs are organised around shifts in idea, time, place or speaker to aid clarity.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest example of using a metaphor in descriptive writing?
options: The night sky was a black ocean drowning every star.
The night sky was dark, with some stars showing.
The night sky looked like it had stars in it.
The night sky was very dark and a bit cloudy.
questions.explain: Calling the sky 'a black ocean' directly identifies it as something else, creating a vivid metaphor.

questions.q: When writing to advise, which tone is usually most effective?
options: Vague and uncertain throughout
Sarcastic and mocking
Aggressive and demanding
Reassuring and constructive, offering clear guidance
questions.explain: Writing to advise works best with a supportive, constructive tone that guides the reader.

questions.q: Which is an effective way to vary sentence length for tension in narrative writing?
options: Follow several longer sentences with a short, punchy one: 'He stopped.'
Use the same length throughout
Avoid full stops entirely
Use only very long sentences
questions.explain: A sudden short sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and tension.

questions.q: What is the best way to structure a piece of persuasive writing for impact?
options: Open with a hook, develop arguments in clear paragraphs, end with a memorable call to action
List random facts in no order
Save the main point for a footnote
Put every idea in one giant paragraph
questions.explain: A strong structure hooks, develops logically and ends with a powerful closing message.

questions.q: You are writing a magazine article. Which feature is most typical of the article form?
options: A signed-off complimentary close like 'Yours sincerely'
An engaging headline and a subheading that draws the reader in
A list of stage directions
A scene number and act heading
questions.explain: Articles use headlines and subheadings to grab attention and signpost content.

questions.q: What does 'planning' your writing before you start mainly help you to do?
options: Make the writing longer
Organise ideas logically and avoid drifting off task
Use up more time
Avoid using paragraphs
questions.explain: Planning structures ideas in advance so the writing stays coherent and on-task.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a fronted adverbial to vary sentence structure?
options: The silence was shattered by the alarm.
Without warning, the alarm shattered the silence.
The alarm shattered the silence.
The alarm was loud and it shattered the silence.
questions.explain: 'Without warning' is an adverbial placed at the front of the sentence for variety and effect.

questions.q: Which sentence opener creates the most engaging, dramatic story opening?
options: My name is Tom and this is my story.
It was a normal day at school.
I am going to tell you about a time I was scared.
The door slammed shut behind me, and the lights went out.
questions.explain: Starting in the middle of the action (in medias res) hooks the reader immediately.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest, most memorable ending to a persuasive piece?
options: That is the end of my writing.
So yeah, that's about it really.
The choice is yours: act now, or watch our future slip away.
I think I have said enough now.
questions.explain: A direct, balanced final appeal leaves a lasting impression on the reader.

questions.q: You are writing a speech. Which feature would make it most engaging for a live audience?
options: A bulleted shopping list
Footnotes and references
A repeated phrase used as a rallying refrain
Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense detail
questions.explain: Repetition (anaphora) builds rhythm and impact, ideal for spoken delivery.
